cls: Adrenergic agonist - non-selective alpha and beta sympathomimetic catecholamine
quick: Anaphylaxis: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL = 1:1000) into anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5-15 min as needed
Use when clearly needed; do not withhold in anaphylaxis or arrest - benefit outweighs risk
Compatible - poor oral bioavailability and short half-life mean negligible infant exposure
BP, heart rate/rhythm (ECG), perfusion; in infusion settings continuous cardiac monitoring
summary: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is an endogenous catecholamine acting on alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. It is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis (given IM) and a key drug in cardiac arrest (given IV/IO), and is used as a vasopressor for shock and as an adjunct to local anesthetics. Effects include increased cardiac contractility and rate, vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, and reduced mucosal edema. CRITICAL: distinguish concentrations - 1 mg/mL (1:1000) for IM anaphylaxis vs 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) for IV cardiac arrest.
indications: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis and other severe allergic reactions (IM)
Hypotension associated with septic shock and other vasodilatory shock
Adjunct to local anesthetics to prolong action and reduce bleeding
Acute severe bronchospasm / croup (nebulized) as applicable

dosage.d: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (0.3-0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL / 1:1000), anterolateral thigh
0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.3 mg, or 0.5 mg in adolescents); 1 mg/mL
0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), max 1 mg
Dilute in 5% dextrose; titrate 0.05-2 mcg/kg/min IV infusion
dosage.n: Infuse into a large vein; wean gradually

admin: Anaphylaxis: give 1 mg/mL (1:1000) by IM injection into the anterolateral thigh - fastest reliable route
Cardiac arrest: give 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) IV/IO - NEVER give 1:1000 undiluted IV
Infusions: dilute in 5% dextrose, infuse into a large vein, use an infusion pump, and avoid extravasation (causes tissue necrosis - treat with phentolamine)
Inspect for discoloration/particulates; do not use if pink, brown, or cloudy
Double-check concentration and dose before administration - look-alike concentrations cause serious errors
moa: A direct-acting non-selective adrenergic agonist. Beta-1 stimulation increases myocardial contractility and heart rate (positive inotropy and chronotropy); beta-2 stimulation causes bronchodilation and vasodilation in skeletal muscle; alpha-1 stimulation causes peripheral vasoconstriction raising blood pressure and reducing mucosal/airway edema. In anaphylaxis it also stabilizes mast cells and reduces mediator release.

absolute: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening emergencies (anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest)
relative: For non-emergency use: narrow-angle glaucoma, serious cardiac arrhythmias, coronary disease, severe hypertension, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma
Use with caution with non-selective beta-blockers (refractory hypotension/severe hypertension)

preg: Limited human data. There are risks to mother and fetus from untreated anaphylaxis or shock, and animal studies showed adverse developmental effects at high doses. Epinephrine should NOT be withheld for the treatment of anaphylaxis or cardiac arrest in pregnancy - the benefit outweighs the risk.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding. It is poorly absorbed orally by the infant and has a very short half-life, resulting in negligible exposure.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required; titrate infusions to clinical effect.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required.

major: Non-selective beta-blockers (may blunt response and cause unopposed alpha effect - severe hypertension/bradycardia; anaphylaxis may be resistant)
Halogenated inhalational anesthetics (sensitize myocardium - serious ventricular arrhythmias)
MAO inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants (potentiate pressor effect)
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently raise blood glucose and lactate; can affect catecholamine assays

rare: Acute limb/digital ischemia from inadvertent injection into digits

monitoring: Perfusion and clinical response (resolution of anaphylaxis, return of circulation)
Serum potassium and glucose with prolonged infusion
counsel: If prescribed an autoinjector, carry two at all times and use immediately at the first signs of a severe allergic reaction
Inject into the outer thigh (can be through clothing); then call emergency services even if you feel better
A second dose may be needed after 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist
Symptoms can recur (biphasic) - seek medical observation after any use
Check expiry and that the solution is clear and colorless
pk: Rapid - IV almost immediate; IM within minutes; SC slower
IM peak plasma within ~10 min (thigh faster than arm/SC)
Brief - clinical effect a few minutes to ~10-20 min; repeat dosing often needed
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light; do not freeze; discard if discolored or contains precipitate
pearls: ANAPHYLAXIS = 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM into the thigh; CARDIAC ARREST = 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) IV - never confuse the two concentrations
IM (not SC) into the anterolateral thigh gives the most rapid, reliable absorption in anaphylaxis
No absolute contraindication when treating a life-threatening reaction
Extravasation causes ischemic necrosis - antidote is local phentolamine infiltration
Patients on non-selective beta-blockers may have refractory anaphylaxis - consider IV glucagon
missed: Not applicable - used acutely in emergencies, not on a maintenance schedule. For self-injectors, administer at the first sign of a severe reaction and seek emergency care.
overdose: Overdose causes severe hypertension (risk of cerebral hemorrhage), pulmonary edema, and arrhythmias (transient bradycardia then tachyarrhythmias). Management is supportive: discontinue, monitor ECG/BP; use rapid-acting vasodilators or alpha-blockers (e.g., phentolamine) for severe hypertension and a beta-blocker (cautiously, with alpha-blockade) or lidocaine/amiodarone for arrhythmias.
